doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Cannonball Adderley and the kiddy record
summary: Phil's view of Cannonball as thoughtful intellectual and root player; Rowe passes his test.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Okay. Interesting. That’s a great story. What did you think of Cannonball and Nat?

Well I love hearing that band because they were roaring and I like the rap on Cannonball’s — onstage. I certainly came to understand that it was a little bit more pat than I wished it, you know. In the early sixties I thought that was ad lib.
I’d like to think that but it probably wasn’t.

It wasn’t. In the late sixties I’m catching a couple of more sets. Now maybe it was ad libbed in the early sixties and then it was pat. But I thought he was far more thoughtful about the music than his fame in the Ramsey Lewis area kind of allowed people to know. He’s sort of seen as one of the springboards of the pop-fusion developments that are going to occur. Nowhere near as important as Miles but he’s there and he lasts until ’75, and his band did go a little bit electric and of course and had its “Mercy Mercy Mercy,” you know a hit. But I saw him as one of the great intellectuals who were also roaring roots players, which is the ultimate combination from a jazz studies point of view. You don’t have to intellectualize this music but if you want to study it you’ve got to know something about it. That kiddy record that Cannonball did, that’s killing.
How come you know so much?
Yeah but Cannonball, a kiddy record.
I have it. PS. You’re a heavyweight. You went up sixty notches. There’s a building here with 7,000 people who think they know that record and they don’t.
That Cannonball kiddy record, you’re one of my new heroes now.
